messages.subject: sd report gradients vs optim
messages.body_plain:
Hi friends,

I'm getting some strange gradients in my sd report as compared to the gradients getting returned by optim().

For example, when optimising, I get a final MGC of ~ 0.09 (you can argue that this is too high, but it's small enough for illustrative purposes).

After optimising, I call sdreport(obj) to calculate standard errors and check if the Hessian (covariance matrix) is PD.

The final gradients after calculating standard errors are sometimes much higher, for some parameters they are around -3, and for two around -20.

I am concerned that the delta method procedure used for calculating standard errors is ending in some strange place. But the Hessian comes out PD and all the standard errors look fine, so I'm not sure what to conclude, except there's something funky going on.

Since I had a covariance matrix to sample initial parameters, I also ran HMC via tmbstan. The resulting posteriors all have reasonable convergence metrics and the marginal densities all look good.

Sam

messages.subject: Different convergence metrics on M1 vs Intel
messages.subject_clean: Different convergence metrics on M1 vs Intel
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gang,

I'm getting some different outputs from the same model, code, and data on different mahcines.

I'm running some retrospective analyses of a fisheries model on two Macs, an M1 Max MBP, and a 2013 garbage can Mac Pro with Intel Xeon processors.

On the M1, I get low gradients during optimisation for point estimates, nice HMC posteriors, etc (albeit with weird gradients after calculating standard errors of MLEs, see https://groups.google.com/g/tmb-users/c/PShnM1ZN7ns/m/oFdQWn2DAAAJ)

On the Intel Mac Pro, there are some cases/peels where the model reaches similar or the same final gradients and parameter estimates, but 1 or all of the SEs are NaN after calculating SD reports.

The two machines are running the same TMB package version, but different R versions (M1 is 4.1.2, Mac Pro is 4.2.0)

Does anyone have any insights into this? Would system architecture be a huge issue here?

messages.subject: Re: sd report gradients vs optim
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam, I think the first thing I'd try is to see if you can use some Newton steps to get those gradients to 0 and see if the problem persists (e.g., in fit_tmb <https://github.com/kaskr/TMB_contrib_R/blob/master/TMBhelper/R/fit_tmb.R#L19>). Do those parameters with large gradients post uncertainty calcs have a much smaller scale relative to the SE? If so could rescaling it help? I have never looked at the gradients like that so don't have a sense of how well they behave in practice, but it does seem concerning if calculation of the Hessian involves something with those gradients. -Cole

messages.subject: Re: Different convergence metrics on M1 vs Intel
messages.subject_clean: Different convergence metrics on M1 vs Intel
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sam, that's not totally unexpected for HMC via tmbstan, because the autodiff gradients are **slightly** different and that slowly diverges and so usually by the end of the chains two architectures can have completely different samples. Kasper found this when building out tmbstan and comparing to Stan. Stan-dev also talks about this in their manual. But I can't see why that would happen with optimization since it's converging to a stable point. Is your model really unstable? Seems like this and the other issue point to some kind of erratic behavior of the model. Do the SEs compare well to posterior marginal SDs for fixed effects? -Cole

messages.subject: AD Hessian calculation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I've been using TMB for about a year for some reasonably complex ecological modelling problems and it has generally worked very well. The model I'm currently working on seems to be having some optimization issues, and frankly I'm not sure if these issues are a result of the R optimx package I'm using for optimization, or TMB itself. Some of the optimization methods within optimx are second-order methods that require the computation (or approximation) of a Hessian. I figured an exact, automatically differentiated Hessian from TMB would be best, so I included likelihood$he as an argument in my optimx call along with likelihood$fn and likelihood$gr.

When I ran this, R returned an error indicating that my Hessian "might be wrong". I looked into this further and apparently optimx runs an internal function, called optimx.check, that compares the user-supplied Hessian function to a numerically derived Hessian (generated by a function in the numDeriv R package). I manually compared the two Hessians and indeed, they are a bit different. I would naturally assume that in truth, the AD-computed Hessian would be more accurate than the numerical Hessian, but I don't have enough experience to know for sure. For what it's worth, in my case, the numerically derived Hessian is symmetric, whereas TMB's Hessian is slightly asymmetric (largest differences on the order of 10^-11).

I know this may be a bit out of the scope of this group, but any thoughts on how to proceed? Maybe it's best to just use the numerically calculated Hessian, but the likelihood function is very noisy so I was thinking an AD-generated Hessian could help. I'm happy to share more information if necessary.

Thank you!
Peter

messages.subject: Re: [TMB users] AD Hessian calculation
messages.body_plain:
Also fairly ignorant, but:

* it's kind of surprising that the AD-generated Hessian is asymmetric. I
can imagine the computations of (i,j) and (j,i) elements being
different, but don't quite understand why AD would bother computing
both?  You might try symmetrizing by computing (H + t(H))/2, that would
be cheap and might help a little bit?

   My limited and out-of-date knowledge of numerical optimization
methods is that people had decided that in general the Hessian-based
algorithms weren't in general sufficiently much better than conjugate
gradients or quasi-Newton methods that it was worth the extra cost of
computing the Hessian.  I don't know if having AD-based rather than
symbolic Hessians changes that calculus or not ...

   If it were me I would try them both out on some test cases and see
how it went ...

messages.subject: Saddlepoint Approximation
messages.body_plain:
Hey Kasper et al,

I've been working for a while with Wei Zhang who has developed methods to fit latent multiomial mark-recapture models using the saddlepoint approximation. His implementation uses a modified version of some of the TMB functions.

We know that there has been an issue about this on github <https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/pull/294> and we saw the recent message saying that the changes had been moved to the main branch. We'd like to be able to modify our code to take advantage of this, so we don't have to modify the code outside of the package. Unfortunately, we're having trouble getting the spa_gauss example <https://github.com/kaskr/adcomp/blob/master/tmb_examples/TMBad/spa_gauss.R> to work. The compiler fails because it's unable to find the TMBad type.

I've copied the start of the error message below and attached the completed log. Can you provide any suggestions for running this example and how to work with the new SPA features?

Many thanks in advance!

Simon
